title: Surdas sings the child Krishna
hookLine: a singer by the river stops singing about himself
carry: vatsalya: loving God as your own child
tomorrow: what does a boy with butter on his face tell his mother?

cards: A singer sits near a river and sings about himself. How low he has fallen. How far he is from God.
How little he deserves. That's how one old account remembers Surdas before his life turned. Tradition says he was blind, and lived beside the Yamuna, in the country of Braj, where Krishna grew up.
One day a teacher named Vallabhacharya stops to listen. He hears the sad songs through. Then he says one thing, and it changes what Surdas sings from then on.

teach.b: The account comes from a book of stories about Vallabha's followers. The teacher says, roughly: why whine like this? Sing about the Lord's play, his lila.
And Surdas does. He turns from his own sorrow to a child's life in a cowherd village.

teach.h: THE SURSAGAR: THE OCEAN OF SUR.
teach.b: The songs carried under his name are called the Sursagar, the ocean of Sur, full of small household things: a cradle, a churn of yogurt, a mother calling her boy in to eat. Here's one.
Little Krishna comes to Yashoda with a complaint.

teach.h: MOTHER, WHEN WILL MY BRAID GROW?
teach.b: Mother, when will my braid grow? You keep telling me to drink my milk and it'll get long and thick like my brother Balarama's. I've drunk and drunk, and it's still short.
A tiny boy comparing hair with his big brother, suspecting his mother of a trick. That's the whole song, and it is a song about God.

teach.h: VATSALYA: LOVING GOD AS YOUR CHILD.
teach.b: Bhakti has a name for this kind of love: vatsalya, the tenderness of a parent for a child.
Instead of looking up at God from far below, the singer stands where Yashoda stands and looks down, at someone small enough to worry about. And it's still how many Hindus pray.
In many homes, a small image of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, is bathed, dressed, fed and put to bed like a child. In Vallabha's tradition, Surdas's songs are sung to Krishna as part of that daily care.

how: Songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna temples and homes in north India, and in the Pushti Marg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya they are part of the daily service before Krishna's image.

s: Surdas sings of Krishna mostly as a grown king
the songs in today's lesson are full of Krishna's childhood in a cowherd village.
in the old account, the teacher told Surdas to stop singing
he told him to change the subject: from his own failings to the Lord's play.
vatsalya is the love of a parent for a child
Surdas sings it from Yashoda's place, looking down at a small boy.

games.q: you're a teacher walking by the river. a singer is singing beautifully about how worthless he is. what do you tell him?
o: sing louder, so more people hear you.
why whine? sing about the Lord's play.
stop singing and go study scripture.
games.why: in the old account, Vallabhacharya tells him, roughly, to stop whining and sing the lila. Surdas turns to Krishna's childhood, and the sad songs give way to a cradle and a churn.

practice: Notice, without arguing, whatever your mind likes to sing about you: what's wrong, what's late, what isn't enough. Then turn, the way the teacher turned Surdas.
If you keep a small shrine, look at the image there the way Yashoda looks at a boy with a short braid, and offer it something small: a sip of water, a sweet, a line of song.
If you don't pray, turn toward someone small in your care and hold them with a little worry and a lot of fondness.

wordCard.voice: Surdas. A singer of Braj who, tradition says, was blind, and who turned from his own sorrow to sing of a child named Krishna.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: the singer's name. the songs carried under it are gathered as the Sursagar.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya, loving God as your own child. The sad song about yourself can make room for someone small. Tomorrow: what does a boy with butter on his face tell his mother?
